abstract: This study uses data from three firms — a car manufacturer (1,800 workers), a quick-service restaurant chain (2,500 workers), and a retailer (25,400 workers) in Argentina and Colombia — to show that middle managers play a critical role in determining employee training participation. Managerial differences significantly influence employee performance and absenteeism, especially during periods of organizational change.
keyFindings: Variation in training participation among employees is closely tied to differences in middle managers' behavior and practices
Middle managers who actively engage with employees and emphasize well-being and development are associated with significantly higher training participation
When a high-training manager takes over a team from a low-training manager, training participation surges within weeks
The managerial traits predicting higher training participation include strong social skills and commitment to developing underperformers
The same training program deployed within the same firm can have different take-up rates depending on an employee's immediate manager
methodology: Analysis of administrative data from three firms: a car manufacturer (1,800 workers), quick-service restaurant chain (2,500 workers), and retailer (25,400 workers) in Argentina and Colombia. Published as NBER Working Paper 33670 and HBS Strategy Unit Working Paper 25-045.
qualifiers: Study is about general workforce training, not AI-specific training. Data is from firms in Argentina and Colombia; organizational dynamics may differ in US context. The study covers three specific firms and may not generalize to all industries.
